title: How This Site Works
abstract: A guided tour of the portfolio, the hourly GitHub Actions pipeline, and the collector that turns trusted feeds into a fresh static news page.
imageAlt: Diagram connecting the portfolio, GitHub Actions, GitHub Pages, and news sources
lede: This portfolio is intentionally small: plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript in the browser, with a focused TypeScript collector doing the heavier work. GitHub supplies the temporary compute, while GitHub Pages only has to serve static files.

sections.heading: The page in one picture
paragraphs: The repository is the source for the site code, portfolio projects, blog posts, and the list of trusted news sources. GitHub Actions checks out that source, refreshes the news, and packages the public folder. GitHub Pages then serves the resulting artifact as an ordinary static website.

sections.heading: How the portfolio page works
paragraphs: The browser first loads a single index page. Navigation switches between About, Resume, Portfolio, Blog, News, and Contact without downloading a new layout each time.

Portfolio entries live in a JSON file. The portfolio script fetches that file, creates one card per project, and adds the preview image, abstract, category, and destination link. The blog follows the same content-first pattern: this article and its preview metadata live in blog JSON, and the interface renders the list or the full article from the current URL.

sections.heading: Why the news can refresh every hour
paragraphs: There is no portfolio server running continuously. The schedule below asks GitHub Actions to create a temporary runner at minute 17 of every hour. The five cron fields mean minute, hour, day of month, month, and day of week, so the four asterisks match every hour and every day.

GitHub evaluates this schedule in UTC because no timezone is specified. Choosing minute 17 also avoids the especially busy start of the hour. Scheduled execution is best effort: GitHub documents that runs can be delayed during heavy load, so hourly means a regular target rather than an exact sixty-minute promise.
The other triggers are useful too. A push to master publishes code or writing changes, while workflow_dispatch adds the Run workflow button in GitHub's Actions interface.

codeBlocks.code:
on:
  push:
    branches:
      - master
  schedule:
    - cron: "17 * * * *"
  workflow_dispatch:

sections.heading: What the GitHub runner does
paragraphs: Each run starts on a clean Ubuntu machine. It checks out the latest repository commit, installs the exact dependency versions from the lockfile, compiles the TypeScript as a build check, and runs the static collector. The public directory is uploaded as a Pages artifact only after those steps succeed.

The deploy job depends on the build job, so it cannot publish a half-built site. Its pages: write and id-token: write permissions are scoped to deployment; the workflow-level contents: read permission is deliberately not enough to commit generated news back into the repository.

codeBlocks.code:
- name: Install dependencies
  run: npm ci

- name: Check TypeScript
  run: npm test

- name: Collect news
  run: npm run collect:static

- name: Upload Pages artifact
  uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
  with:
    path: public

# A separate job publishes that artifact.
- name: Deploy to GitHub Pages
  uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4

bullets: Pushes make code and writing updates visible.
The schedule refreshes news even when nobody changes the repository.
A manual run is available when an immediate collection is useful.
Concurrent runs are cancelled so only the newest Pages deployment finishes.

sections.heading: How one source becomes news cards
paragraphs: The collector reads config/sources.txt one URL at a time. It first tries to parse the response as RSS, Atom, or JSON Feed. If the response is a webpage, it looks for a linked feed; if no usable structured feed exists, it extracts article candidates from the HTML.

The normalized list is capped at 30 candidates per source by default. Four workers then verify article pages concurrently. Confirmed HTTP 404 or 410 responses and pages whose title or main heading looks like a soft 404 are removed.

For a valid HTML article, the collector recovers missing publication dates from metadata, JSON-LD, time elements, visible dates, or a date-shaped URL. It also examines social and article images, but keeps a preview only after downloading it and measuring a width greater than 480 pixels.

sections.heading: The deployed feed is a fresh snapshot
paragraphs: The static collector deliberately opens an in-memory SQLite database. It does not import the previously deployed JSON file, so each workflow run rebuilds the digest from the articles currently returned by the configured sources. Canonical URLs and stable hashes prevent duplicates inside that run, but first-seen timestamps and internal row IDs begin again on the next runner.

That makes the News page a current digest rather than a permanent archive. The generated items.json is placed in the Pages artifact, not committed to the repository. If every source fails and no items are collected, the script throws before deployment, leaving the last successful Pages artifact live. A partial source failure does not stop deployment, so that source can be absent until a later successful run.

sections.heading: How the browser gets the new deployment
paragraphs: GitHub Pages serves public/content/information/items.json like any other static asset. When the News tab opens, the browser adds a unique query value and requests the file with no-store caching, then builds the source filter and article cards from the response.

The Reload button repeats that browser request; it does not trigger GitHub Actions or contact the news sites directly. Therefore a newly published article appears after the next successful collection and Pages deployment, followed by a page load or Reload in the visitor's browser.

sections.heading: Why this architecture
paragraphs: There is no application server to keep alive in production and no database required by visitors. GitHub provides short-lived compute for collection, and GitHub Pages serves ordinary static files. The result is inexpensive, portable, and resilient, while the local Fastify server and persistent SQLite database remain useful during development.

The trade-off is latency and limited history: updates arrive when a scheduled workflow and deployment finish, rather than instantly, and the static output reflects the sources' current windows. In return, each live artifact is associated with a visible workflow run and repository commit without giving the collector permission to rewrite the repository.
